summary.text: A bacteriophage, or phage, is a virus that infects and replicates within bacteria, and its name joins a Greek word meaning to devour with the word bacteria.
Phages are proteins wrapped around a DNA or RNA genome, and they are found wherever bacteria exist, among the most common and diverse entities in the biosphere.
Phages have been used as an alternative to antibiotics, and they are seen as a possible therapy against multi-drug-resistant strains of many bacteria.

facts.label: How they infect
facts.value: They inject their genome into a bacterium's cytoplasm

facts.label: Named by
facts.value: Félix d'Hérelle, who called it a bacterium-eater

facts.label: Genome size
facts.value: As few as four genes, up to hundreds

facts.label: Ocean reach
facts.value: Up to 70% of marine bacteria may be infected

items.prompt: A phage touches a bacterium and injects its genome. Where does the phage's copying then take place?

options.label: In the water around the bacterium's outer wall
Inside the bacterium it has infected
On the phage's own surface, away from the bacterium
In the nearest cell of a plant or animal

items.explain: Phages replicate within the bacterium after injecting their genome into its cytoplasm.

items.prompt: Phage treatments were used in places from the 1920s. Why did they fade in much of the world once antibiotics arrived?

options.label: Every phage trial showed that the treatment was unsafe
Phages could no longer be found in any natural place
Antibiotics were first discovered by the same scientist
Antibiotics were easier to make, store and prescribe

items.explain: Antibiotics were widely marketed and were easier to make, store and prescribe, while phage trials raised questions and Soviet research was little followed abroad.

items.prompt: A researcher says phages are rare curiosities. What undermines that claim?

options.label: They live wherever bacteria do and likely outnumber all organisms combined
They are found only in sewers and cannot spread to other places
They are rare in the ocean and common only on dry land
They are too tiny for there to be very many of them

items.explain: Phages are ubiquitous, found wherever bacteria exist, with an estimated number greater than every living organism on Earth combined.

items.prompt: Experiments with a bacteria-infecting virus gave convincing evidence about what carries heredity. What was it?

options.label: Protein, rather than DNA, was the genetic material
Fats and sugars together carried the information
DNA, rather than protein, was the genetic material
Both protein and DNA copy themselves on their own

items.explain: Hershey's work, part of the Hershey-Chase experiment, provided convincing evidence that DNA, not protein, was the genetic material of life.

items.prompt: A microbiologist sees clear spots appear on a bacterial culture and cannot see anything causing them. What did d'Hérelle conclude?

options.label: A chemical in the culture dish had eaten the bacteria
An invisible virus that lives on bacteria made them
A larger animal had eaten the bacteria overnight
The bacteria had simply died of old age

items.explain: D'Hérelle understood in a flash that the clear spots were caused by an invisible microbe, a virus parasitic on bacteria, which he called a bacteriophage.

items.prompt: A trial of a phage mix on leg ulcers showed safety but not benefit. What did the authors suggest may explain this?

options.label: Phages cannot survive in any human tissue at all
The patients were given far too few phages to matter
The trial was stopped early by the regulator
Chemicals in standard wound care may have interfered with the phages

items.explain: The authors said certain chemicals in standard wound care, such as lactoferrin or silver, may have interfered with bacteriophage viability.
